response.message:
Improve activation by identifying where new users get stuck, defining a meaningful product-specific value milestone, and designing onboarding that helps them reach it quickly through relevant guidance and hands-on starting points. Use user feedback and funnel experiments to find and address the biggest sources of friction. [S1] [S3] [S5] [S9]

## Find the activation problem and define success

Walk through the experience as a new user and identify where it is confusing or where people stop. Choose an experience-based aha or activation milestone: a good-enough taste of the product’s value, rather than merely logging in or reaching an arbitrary high usage count. Start with a few candidate milestones and check whether they correlate with long-term retention; correlation is useful for focusing, but experimentation is needed to establish causation.

[S1] [S9] [S11]

## Help users reach value quickly

Reduce friction and provide a warm start: let users do something useful rather than only telling or showing them what to do. Ask a small number of targeted questions about their use case, then guide them to relevant templates or sample content they can use immediately. Tailor the landing experience to what users are trying to accomplish, and avoid exposing the product’s full complexity all at once. For example, Miro’s onboarding asks what the user wants to do and quickly provides a matching template; the guest describes reaching use of the template in about five minutes as a good time-to-value standard. Email can also bring users back if they do not start in the product.

[S1] [S2] [S7]

## Use evidence to prioritize and improve the funnel

Study the funnel to find where the largest losses occur, investigate why users leave at those steps, and test changes against the biggest opportunities. Combine behavioral data with qualitative feedback: after more than 10 tests failed to improve a download step, LogMeIn asked registrants who had not downloaded why; many said the free product seemed too good to be true. Showing that a paid trial was also available, with a prominent check mark beside the free version, improved download rate by 300%. More generally, the guest describes two conversion levers: increase the right desire and reduce friction.

[S3] [S4] [S5]

## Make the milestone fit the product

Activation may involve team value, not just an individual action. At GitLab, an aha milestone was two users using two features within the first 14 days: inviting a coworker indicated value to the first user, while shared use of multiple features reflected collaboration. At Snyk, activation meant a team fixing vulnerabilities within 30 days—not merely logging in or finding vulnerabilities—and the definition was tied to downstream retention. These are examples, not universal thresholds; choose a milestone suited to the product and the time it realistically takes users to experience value.

Acquisition tracks bringing users in; activation tracks whether they reach meaningful product value; retention tracks whether they continue using or paying over time. Activation and acquisition can be tested quickly, while retention takes longer to observe and is more complex. [S1] [S2] [S7] [S4]

## Acquisition

Acquisition is about getting more users into the product. The evidence describes user count as a possible growth goal and characterizes acquisition as a major lever, but does not specify a particular acquisition metric such as a channel-level or cost metric.

[S1] [S2] [S10]

## Activation

Activation measures whether new users or teams reach meaningful value—not merely sign in. It is often a relatively quick milestone to test. For example, Snyk defined team activation around fixing vulnerabilities within 30 days, while Airtable used teams with multiple people active and contributing in week four. These milestones were selected because they correlated with downstream retention; the exact definition depends on the product.

[S1] [S6] [S7]

## Retention

Retention measures continued use or paid continuation over a longer period, making it harder to assess quickly: users can stop using or cancel at any time. It can be measured through continued engagement or retention cohorts, and, for subscribers, renewals and expansion. At Snyk, retention meant teams continuing to fix vulnerabilities, not just logging in. Activation and retention are related, but they are not the same metric.

## Make discovery continuous and customer-centered

Torres defines continuous discovery as building ongoing customer feedback loops into product work. Because digital products keep evolving and teams continuously decide what to build, customers should be included continuously too. She says this can be as little as one interview a week for discovering opportunities. [S1, S4]

[S1] [S4]

## Discover and deliver in parallel

Treat backlog items as bets whether or not they have been researched. Discovery helps improve those bets; it should not become a gate that stops delivery until everything is fully discovered. Keep delivering while starting discovery in parallel, adjusting how much discovery you do to the risk and business context. [S2, S5]

[S2] [S5]

## Use interviews and assumption tests for different purposes

Torres describes two core discovery activities: qualitative interviewing to learn about opportunities—customers’ unmet needs, pain points, and desires—and assumption testing to evaluate specific solution assumptions. Observation can be a better way to identify opportunities, but she focuses on interviews because many teams can sustain them week over week. [S6, S3]

[S6] [S3]

## Keep interviews conversational and grounded in real stories

Avoid relying on long, scripted question lists. Make the conversation natural, invite a customer to recount a specific recent experience, set the scene, and follow the timeline with prompts such as “What happened next?” Listen for friction and probe it for detail; summarizing what you heard can help bring the person back to a moment worth exploring. Break ideas into underlying assumptions, prioritize which assumptions to test, and run tests small enough to evaluate one assumption rather than testing an entire idea with a costly, slow experiment. She presents this as a shift in habits and methods—not as a guaranteed cadence for every team. [S3, S9]

[S3] [S9]

## Start with accessible customers

If formal access or permission is a barrier, Torres suggests beginning with people in your network who are like your customers. Her example is a healthcare-badges team that started by talking to a product manager’s doctor uncles. [S10]

# Why Retention Matters More Than Acquisition for Sustainable Growth

Acquisition can make a customer base look bigger. Retention determines whether that growth holds together.

For founders and growth teams, this difference matters: adding users is not the same as building a durable business. **Retention is often the stronger foundation for sustainable growth because it preserves the value already won, amplifies other growth drivers, and can improve what a company can afford to spend to find new customers.** That does not make acquisition optional. It means the two should be managed as connected parts of a growth system—not treated as interchangeable ways to raise a headline number. [S1] [S2] [S7]

## 1. Retention turns a customer base into a compounding asset

A growth model can make the importance of retention more visible than intuition alone. Dan Hockenmaier describes how a company’s growth may be more sensitive to customer retention than teams expect. Retained customers interact with other important drivers: referrals, content generation, and contribution margin. As a result, a modest improvement in retention can be more valuable than a larger change in another area. [S1]

This is the core reason retention can matter more than acquisition: **an acquired customer is not only a one-time addition. What that customer does next can affect the value of the broader growth system.** For products used daily, the retention of existing users who have formed a habitual pattern is particularly important; that continued use can build the habit over time. [S3]

The contrast is churn. If customers leave, acquisition has to keep supplying replacements just to maintain the base. One example discussed in the evidence notes that at 70% annual cohort retention, a company may need to rebuild its user base every three or four years. The point is not that every business has the same retention target. It is that losses accumulate, and a growth plan that overlooks them can misread how much new acquisition is needed to sustain its position. [S8]

**Synthesis:** Think of acquisition as filling a container and retention as reducing the leak. A team can increase the inflow, but persistent churn makes that effort less durable. The analogy is a way to understand the relationship, not a claim that every product’s growth can be reduced to one metric. The useful question is not only “How many users did we add?” but also “What happens to the people we already brought in?”

## 2. Retention can make acquisition more valuable

Retention and acquisition are not rival departments in a zero-sum contest. A stronger relationship with existing customers can change the economics of bringing in new ones.

Thumbtack’s marketplace experience illustrates the connection. Customers often arrived through a search for one specific local service. It could be difficult to encourage them to use additional service categories, but doing so could substantially increase their lifetime value. That higher value, in turn, affected how much the company could afford to pay to acquire customers. The growth model helped the team see that it had concentrated resources on top-of-funnel SEO and conversion, while doing less work on cross-selling and the broader customer journey. It then shifted resources deeper into that journey. [S2]

The lesson is not “stop acquiring.” It is **make acquisition work in partnership with the experience that follows it**. If new customers do not find enough value to return, buy again, refer others, or otherwise contribute to the product’s growth, the acquisition engine has less to build on. In a product-led model, users need to be activated and engaged before their use can support habitual behavior, referrals, or content that attracts further users. [S4]

**Synthesis:** Before increasing acquisition spend, examine whether the product is turning newly acquired users into engaged customers—and whether existing customers have reasons to continue or deepen their relationship. This helps teams consider acquisition not just as a volume problem, but as an investment whose value depends partly on what the product delivers afterward. It does not establish a universal budget formula; the evidence shows the connection, not a fixed ratio between retention and acquisition.

## 3. Put retention first without making it the only priority

“Retention matters more” is a useful corrective when a team treats growth as a constant hunt for new users. It becomes misleading if it turns into “retention is all that matters.” Enduring growth requires both market-share and wallet-share engines, along with acquisition, monetization, and retention. Attention need not be split equally at every moment, but teams should consider the engines together and make deliberate trade-offs. [S7]

That distinction matters for practical decisions. A company may need to focus on getting customers, helping them realize value, earning revenue, or encouraging ongoing use. The appropriate emphasis can change. Retention is a priority because it supports durable growth; it is not a substitute for acquiring customers or creating a viable business model. [S7]

Product type also changes where the team should look. For a product with daily use, the retention of established users and the habits they form may be central. Grammarly provides a counterexample to a universal rule: users do not proactively open it every day, so installation and the activation “aha” moment were described as especially critical. [S3]

**Synthesis:** Avoid adopting a retention metric as a doctrine detached from how the product is used. First ask what continued value looks like for this product. It might involve returning frequently, completing an initial setup that carries a user forward, or using additional parts of a service. The evidence supports tailoring the focus to product behavior; it does not provide a single retention definition or benchmark that applies to every company.

## 4. Improve the experience, not just the reminders

Retention can be hard to move because it reflects the whole product experience. Hockenmaier cautions against going straight to more email or push notifications as a way to improve a retention metric. Instead, teams should understand the customer journey and identify what matters to customers. In a marketplace, that may involve the depth of supply or the customer’s interaction with that supply; more broadly, the work may belong in core product improvements rather than growth messaging alone. [S9]

A practical investigation can begin with questions such as:

- **Where does the customer first experience value?** For some products, the activation or installation moment may carry particular weight. [S3]
- **What does the customer come back to do?** For habitual products, examine whether existing users continue the pattern of use that makes the product valuable. [S3]
- **What happens along the customer journey before someone leaves?** Look for experience issues and product opportunities rather than assuming that another reminder will solve the problem. [S9]
- **Can existing customers gain value from more of the product?** Thumbtack’s cross-category opportunity shows how broader use can affect lifetime value and acquisition economics. [S2]

These are diagnostic prompts, not a guaranteed recipe. Retention reflects multiple parts of the experience, so the evidence does not promise that a particular change will improve it or specify how quickly a team should expect results. [S1] [S9]

## The takeaway: grow the base you acquire

Acquisition brings customers in; retention helps make their value last and can strengthen the system that attracts more. That is why retention often deserves more attention than teams instinctively give it. But sustainable growth is not a choice between keeping customers and finding new ones. It requires understanding how acquisition, product value, ongoing use, and monetization work together. [S1] [S7]

**Practical next step — synthesis:** Build or revisit a growth model that makes retention visible alongside acquisition. Identify how customer retention connects to referrals, content, contribution margin, or lifetime value in your product; then inspect the customer journey for a concrete product experience to improve. Use the model to choose where attention belongs now, rather than assuming either acquisition or retention should always receive the most resources. [S1] [S2] [S9]

artifact.title: How to Learn from Failed Growth Experiments: Make Every Test Answer a Question
artifact.content:
# How to Learn from Failed Growth Experiments: Make Every Test Answer a Question

A growth experiment can miss its target and still be worth running. The real waste is not simply a result that fails to drive revenue. It is a test that leaves the team no wiser—and allows the same unproven idea to return again and again.

For growth teams, the useful question is not only, “Did this work?” It is: **Did we design the test well enough to learn something we can act on?** That shift makes room for unsuccessful outcomes without treating every miss as a meaningful lesson. [S1]

## 1. Redefine what counts as failure

Sri Batchu says that, in his experience, growth experiments have a success rate of roughly 30%. Most of the experiments he encountered did not work. His distinction is important: failure is not merely that a test did not drive revenue; **failure is not learning from the test**. A team can accept unsuccessful outcomes without treating them as pointless, provided the experiment produces a useful lesson. [S1] [S2]

That changes what a team should celebrate. Celebrating every unsuccessful result would be empty if the test was too weak to answer its question. But dismissing every miss as wasted effort ignores what a clear negative result can rule out. The standard is not “Did we win?” or even “Did we try?” It is: **Can we explain what this result tells us about the hypothesis?** This is a synthesis of Batchu’s emphasis on learning through a well-designed, conclusive test. [S1]

This matters when an idea feels intuitively promising. Batchu warns that without a conclusive test, teams can revisit the same idea for years as new people propose it. The organization has neither established that the idea works nor learned enough to stop trying. A decisive miss can help interrupt that cycle; an ambiguous result can keep it alive. [S1] [S2]

## 2. Design the test to answer the question

A test cannot produce a clear lesson simply because it has been labeled an experiment. Batchu identifies two ways to make an experiment successful as a test: have a very large sample, or have a very significant treatment. In B2B, he notes, teams may not have the luxury of a large sample. His recommendation is therefore to maximize the treatment effect: put the tactics and resources that could move the outcome behind the hypothesis. [S1] [S3]

In practical terms, ask whether the tested version gives the idea a serious chance to show an effect. If a team believes several tactics could move a result, testing only a faint version may leave the central question unresolved. A weak intervention that does not work does not necessarily establish that the underlying idea is ineffective. This is an interpretation of Batchu’s stronger-test recommendation, not a separate experimental rule. [S3]

Before launch, a team can ask:

- **What hypothesis are we trying to test?**
- **Which tactics and resources do we believe could move the result?**
- **Can we use a large sample, or should we strengthen the treatment instead?**
- **If the strongest version does not work, what decision will the result support?**

The purpose is not to make every test bigger or more expensive. It is to avoid spending time on a version so limited that its result cannot settle the question. Batchu’s guidance is to put the strongest plausible version behind the hypothesis, then assess its cost and value after learning whether it works. [S3]

## 3. Treat a miss as a decision point

A strong test creates two useful paths. If the full treatment does not work, the team has a clearer basis for deciding not to retry the same idea. If it does work, the result creates a reason to test a more focused version, using fewer tactics or selecting the tactics the team believes worked better. Batchu describes this sequence as a way to optimize over time. [S3]

This is not a promise that one test will explain every detail. It is a way to make the next decision more informed. A negative outcome can help the team stop investing in an idea that did not work even in its strongest version. A positive outcome can open a follow-up question: which parts are necessary, and can the result be achieved with fewer tactics? Each outcome gives the next experiment a clearer purpose. [S3]

**Practical synthesis:** after a test, separate three things:

- **The outcome:** What happened compared with what the team expected?
- **The decision:** Should the team stop, repeat, or refine the approach?
- **The next question:** If continuing, what should the next version isolate or change?

This structure helps prevent “we tried it” from becoming the only record of a test. It also keeps the team honest. If the treatment was not strong enough to answer the hypothesis, the right conclusion may be that the test was inconclusive—not that the idea has been disproved. That distinction follows from the emphasis on designing a test that can fail conclusively. [S1] [S3]

## 4. Look for surprising losers, not only winners

A result can be valuable because it differs sharply from what the team expected. Ronny Kohavi describes a surprising experiment as one where the estimated result beforehand and the actual result differ by a lot. That can mean an expected improvement was flat, or an expectedly modest result was unexpectedly strong—or very negative. He emphasizes examining surprising losers, not just winners. [S5]

The practical implication is that a negative result deserves interpretation, not merely a red mark in a results table. If a test seemed like an obvious improvement but performed very negatively, the gap between expectation and outcome may point to an assumption worth examining. In Kohavi’s example, an indexing change improved relevance but harmed battery life. Looking only at relevance would have missed another outcome that moved in the opposite direction. [S5]

The bounded lesson is to compare what changed with what you expected, including results that appear disappointing or mixed. The evidence does not specify which metrics every team should use, or how to resolve competing outcomes. Those choices depend on the experiment. What it does support is the value of noticing large expectation-result gaps and investigating surprising negative outcomes. [S5]

## 5. Make the learning visible

Learning that stays in one team’s notes has limited reach. Kohavi describes quarterly meetings focused on the most surprising experiments and observes that companies can launch many experiments without returning to summarize what they learned. His emphasis is institutional learning: make results available for reflection, not just record experiment volume. [S5]

Ben Williams likewise says insights from growth teams can be useful beyond growth, and people cannot use them if they are not shared. He describes socializing learnings widely and visibly, including those from mistakes and failures. [S8]

**Practical synthesis:** a concise learning note can include:

- The hypothesis and treatment that were tested.
- What the team expected and what happened.
- Whether the result answers the question or remains inconclusive.
- What decision follows, and what others may be able to use.

The point is not to turn every experiment into a long report. It is to keep a clear lesson from disappearing and give others a chance to apply it. Sharing can also help the organization recognize when an old idea is being proposed again and examine what previous tests established. That is a synthesis of the advice to fail conclusively and socialize learning. [S1] [S8]

## The limits—and the next step

The evidence offers principles, not a complete experimentation manual. It does not specify how to calculate sample size, choose metrics, define statistical significance, or decide how long a test should run. Nor does maximizing a treatment guarantee a conclusive answer in every situation. These recommendations are not a substitute for sound measurement or experiment-specific judgment.

Still, the central practice is clear: **design the test to answer a question, interpret the result against expectations, and share what the team learned.** The next time an experiment misses its goal, do not stop at “it failed.” Write down whether the test was strong enough to answer its hypothesis. If it was, state the decision the result supports. If it was not, identify what made the result inconclusive before repeating the idea.

That is how a failed experiment becomes more than an unsuccessful attempt: it becomes a usable answer for the next decision. [S1] [S3] [S5] [S8]
